approaches.name: Arthroscopic approach for selected distal femoral articular fractures
approaches.region: knee and distal femoral articular surface
approaches.corridor: Standard anterolateral viewing and anteromedial working portals adjacent to the patellar tendon

sources.title: Surgical approaches and outcomes associated with intra-articular Hoffa fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A young patient has a minimally or nondisplaced articular fracture suitable for arthroscopy-assisted assessment and fixation by an experienced knee arthroscopist

positioning.text: Position supine with a thigh holder or post, the knee freely flexible, and the distal femur accessible for percutaneous fixation and fluoroscopy.

setup.text: Use only with advanced arthroscopic expertise; prepare pump irrigation, full knee arthroscopy instruments, percutaneous fixation tools, and fluoroscopy before portal placement.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark patella, patellar tendon borders, medial and lateral joint lines, femoral condyles, and standard soft spots adjacent to the tendon.

incision.text: Create approximately 5-mm anterolateral and anteromedial stab incisions at the palpated soft spots adjacent to the patellar tendon.

superficial_interval.text: Spread portal tracts bluntly through capsule while protecting skin nerves and the patellar tendon; establish the medial portal under direct arthroscopic control.

deep_interval.text: Insert the anterolateral cannula gently into the joint, replace the blunt trocar with the scope, clear hemarthrosis, and use the medial portal for probing and controlled instrumentation.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, retinacular capsule at standard portals, synovium, then the knee articular cavity and distal femoral surface.

structures_encountered.text: Patellar tendon, fat pad, synovium, patellofemoral and tibiofemoral cartilage, menisci, cruciate ligaments, and fracture surface are examined.

structures_at_risk.text: Articular cartilage, menisci, cruciate ligaments, patellar tendon, portal-adjacent sensory branches, and posterior neurovascular structures are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Never advance a sharp trocar or drill across the joint without direct visualization; monitor fluid extravasation because fracture planes can communicate with thigh compartments.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forcing instruments against cartilage or using portal leverage to compensate for poor trajectory; create an accessory portal under visualization when required.

exposure.text: Provides magnified assessment of articular reduction and permits a complete survey for meniscal, ligament, and osteochondral injuries with minimal arthrotomy.

limitations.text: Recommended only for selected minimally displaced patterns; comminution, displaced columns, limited fixation options, and fluid extravasation constrain its use.

extensions.text: Add image-guided accessory portals or convert to an open parapatellar or condylar exposure when direct reduction, buttressing, or fragment control is inadequate.

indications.text: Consider for minimally or nondisplaced intra-articular distal femoral fractures in young patients when arthroscopy can verify congruity and associated soft-tissue injury.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid in displaced or highly comminuted fractures requiring open reduction, major capsular disruption with uncontrolled extravasation, active infection, or when arthroscopic expertise is unavailable.

implant_implications.text: Choose percutaneous screw trajectories that compress the fracture while remaining outside weight-bearing cartilage and clear of cruciate attachments and the notch.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Combine arthroscopic surface assessment with orthogonal and tangential imaging to verify fragment position, screw trajectory, length, and absence of intra-articular prominence.

closure.text: Drain irrigation fluid as appropriate, confirm hemostasis and compartment softness, and close portal skin incisions routinely.

complications.text: Complications include chondral injury, fluid extravasation and compartment syndrome, missed instability, infection, fixation loss, stiffness, neurovascular injury, and post-traumatic arthritis.

bailouts.text: If visualization deteriorates, extravasation progresses, or stable anatomic reduction cannot be obtained, stop pump inflow and convert promptly to the appropriate open exposure.

questions.question: Which fractures are candidates for this approach?
questions.answer: Selected minimally or nondisplaced articular fractures in young patients.

questions.question: What examination must accompany fracture assessment?
questions.answer: A complete knee arthroscopy for meniscal, ligament, and osteochondral injuries.

questions.question: Where are the standard portals?
questions.answer: At the anterolateral and anteromedial soft spots adjacent to the patellar tendon.

approaches.name: Gerdy-tubercle osteotomy approach for a lateral Hoffa fracture
approaches.region: lateral knee and posterior lateral femoral condyle
approaches.corridor: Extended lateral knee exposure with osteotomy of the iliotibial-band insertion at Gerdy tubercle to reach the posterior lateral condyle

sources.title: Coronal plane partial articular fractures of the distal femoral condyle

procedure_applications.condition: A lateral Hoffa fragment requires posterior articular access and posterior-to-anterior lag-screw or buttress fixation

positioning.text: Position supine with a bump or lateral tilt and the knee freely flexible so the lateral and posterior condyle can be accessed and imaged.

setup.text: Review thin-cut CT for fragment morphology, plan osteotomy fixation before incision, and prepare direct posterior-condyle reduction, lag-screw, and buttress options.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark patella, joint line, fibular head, Gerdy tubercle, iliotibial band, lateral epicondyle, and peroneal-nerve course.

incision.text: Use a lateral knee incision centered over the distal iliotibial band and Gerdy tubercle, extending proximally and distally for the planned osteotomy and condylar access.

superficial_interval.text: Expose the iliotibial-band insertion as a repairable unit, preserve lateral sensory tissue, and identify the posterolateral danger zone before osteotomy.

deep_interval.text: Create and mobilize a controlled Gerdy-tubercle osteotomy with the iliotibial-band attachment, then develop the lateral capsular interval to the posterior lateral femoral condyle.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, iliotibial band and Gerdy insertion, osteotomy fragment, lateral capsule and posterolateral soft tissues, then posterior lateral condyle.

structures_encountered.text: Iliotibial band, Gerdy tubercle, lateral capsule, lateral meniscus, lateral collateral and popliteus region, posterior condylar cartilage, and Hoffa fragment are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Common peroneal nerve, popliteal vessels, lateral meniscus, popliteus, lateral collateral complex, articular cartilage, and osteotomy fragment are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Posterior dissection and posterior-to-anterior drilling approach the popliteal bundle; maintain direct bony contact, guarded depth, and fluoroscopic control.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forceful posterolateral retraction that tensions the peroneal nerve or collateral structures, and protect the meniscus and cartilage from retractors.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to the posterior lateral condylar articular surface and enables posterior-to-anterior lag-screw placement or posterior buttressing.

limitations.text: This specialized approach adds an osteotomy requiring repair and is not appropriate for medial Hoffa fragments or fractures adequately exposed by a standard parapatellar route.

extensions.text: Extend proximally along the lateral distal femur or combine with a parapatellar arthrotomy when broader anterior articular visualization is required.

indications.text: Use selectively for a lateral coronal-plane Hoffa fracture when posterior fragment visualization and posterior-to-anterior fixation cannot be achieved safely through a simpler exposure.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid for medial condylar fragments, inadequate Gerdy-tubercle bone, compromised lateral soft tissue, or when an alternative approach provides equivalent access without osteotomy.

implant_implications.text: Plan posterior-to-anterior lag screws perpendicular to the fracture, add a buttress when shear demands it, and securely refix the Gerdy osteotomy without joint penetration.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use AP, lateral, oblique, and tangential condylar views to confirm articular reduction, posterior screw start and length, and osteotomy fixation.

closure.text: Repair the capsule and any released lateral structures, anatomically reduce and fix the Gerdy fragment with the iliotibial band tension restored, then close fascia and skin.

complications.text: Complications include peroneal or popliteal injury, osteotomy nonunion or displacement, articular malreduction, stiffness, ligament or meniscal injury, infection, and post-traumatic arthritis.

bailouts.text: If posterior visualization remains unsafe, add a complementary exposure or revise fixation direction rather than drilling blindly toward the popliteal fossa.

questions.question: What fracture is the classic indication?
questions.answer: A lateral femoral-condyle Hoffa fracture needing posterior fixation.

questions.question: What structure remains attached to the osteotomy fragment?
questions.answer: The iliotibial band at Gerdy tubercle.

questions.question: Why use posterior-to-anterior screws?
questions.answer: They can be placed perpendicular to the coronal fracture plane and provide compression.

approaches.name: Lateral anterolateral approach to the distal femur
approaches.region: lateral distal thigh and distal femur
approaches.corridor: Lateral iliotibial-band incision with distal-to-proximal vastus-lateralis elevation and optional lateral arthrotomy

sources.title: Lateral anterolateral approach to the distal femur
Surgical approaches to the lateral knee
Current concepts in the treatment of distal femur fractures in adults

procedure_applications.condition: A simple lateral articular or extra-articular distal femur fracture requires direct lateral reduction and plate fixation

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with a bump under the ipsilateral hip and the knee flexed enough to relax gastrocnemius and permit lateral imaging.

setup.text: Prepare the entire limb, review CT for articular extensions, plan plate length, and ensure unobstructed AP, lateral, and oblique imaging.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark femoral shaft, lateral epicondyle, joint line, patella, Gerdy tubercle, iliotibial band, and fibular head.

incision.text: Begin in the midlateral thigh at the needed proximal level, curve over the lateral condyle, and extend toward Gerdy tubercle when arthrotomy is required; stop just distal to the joint line if it is not.

superficial_interval.text: Divide the iliotibial band once in line with its fibers and the incision to preserve clean edges for repair.

deep_interval.text: Incise vastus-lateralis fascia just anterior to the lateral intermuscular septum, elevate muscle from distal to proximal, ligate perforators, and retract the muscle anteromedially.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, iliotibial band, vastus-lateralis fascia, muscle-septum interval and perforators, lateral periosteum, and optional lateral capsule.

structures_encountered.text: Iliotibial band, vastus lateralis, lateral intermuscular septum, profunda perforators, lateral femur, joint capsule, patellar tendon, and lateral meniscus are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Profunda femoris perforators, periosteal blood supply, lateral superior genicular vessels, lateral meniscus, patellar tendon, and articular cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Identify and ligate perforators during proximal elevation and avoid posterior blind dissection across the septum toward the popliteal neurovascular bundle.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract vastus lateralis atraumatically and avoid excessive tension on the patellar tendon during arthrotomy, particularly in osteoporotic bone.

exposure.text: Exposes the lateral distal femur for reduction and plate placement; an optional anterior-third lateral arthrotomy visualizes simple articular fractures.

limitations.text: Medial-condyle and complex complete-articular patterns are poorly visualized and are generally better served by a parapatellar or broader articular exposure.

extensions.text: Extend proximally along the lateral femoral shaft and distally into a lateral arthrotomy as dictated by fracture and plate length.

indications.text: Use for extra-articular fractures and simple lateral articular patterns that can be reduced and plated from the lateral side.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose a parapatellar or alternative exposure for complex bicondylar, medial-condylar, posterior, or highly comminuted articular injuries needing broader visualization.

implant_implications.text: Center the lateral plate on the distal femur, preserve periosteum, obtain appropriate distal subchondral and proximal fixation, and avoid notch or joint penetration.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm mechanical and anatomic alignment, condylar width, articular congruity, plate position, and screw containment on AP, lateral, and oblique views.

closure.text: Close arthrotomy, repair vastus-lateralis fascia, precisely reapproximate iliotibial band, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include perforator bleeding, muscle or periosteal devascularization, malalignment, articular malreduction, stiffness, patellar-tendon injury, infection, nonunion, and hardware irritation.

bailouts.text: If medial or posterior articular reduction cannot be assessed, add or convert to a parapatellar or fragment-specific exposure rather than accepting unseen malreduction.

questions.question: Where is vastus lateralis elevated?
questions.answer: From the lateral intermuscular septum, working distal to proximal and retracting it anteromedially.

questions.question: Which vessels commonly require ligation?
questions.answer: Perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery and vein.

questions.question: When can the distal skin incision stop above Gerdy tubercle?
questions.answer: When no arthrotomy or direct joint visualization is required.
